title: 88 students bag first class degrees as UNIOSUN holds 16th convocation
content:
By Shina Abubakar
As Osun State University (UNIOSUN), Osogbo, holds its 16th convocation ceremony, 88 students across different faculties will be graduating with first-class degrees.
Speaking with journalists at the university’s multi-purpose hall in Osogbo on Saturday, the Vice-Chancellor, Professor Clement Adebooye, said a total of 4,357 students would be awarded different categories of degrees in both undergraduate and postgraduate programmes.
He added that out of the stated figure of graduating students, 3,845 will be graduating in the first degree programmes across faculties, nine students will graduate with postgraduate diplomas, 400 with master’s degrees and 100 successfully bagged their Doctors of Philosophy, PhDs.
“The 16th Convocation of our great University is not merely a ceremony for the conferment of degrees and diplomas. It is an opportunity to celebrate scholarship, resilience, innovation, character and the transformative power of education. I am particularly delighted to announce that a total of 4,357 first degrees, postgraduate diplomas and higher degrees will be awarded at this year’s Convocation Ceremonies.
“In the undergraduates programmes, 88 students graduated with First honours, 1,509 graduated with second class (upper division), 1,946 bagged second class (lower division), 220 bagged third class while three students graduated with pass degrees.
“These figures reflect the University’s sustained commitment to providing quality education and producing graduates who are fully equipped with the knowledge, skills and character required to contribute meaningfully to national and global development,” he added.
Professor Adebooye also disclosed that the university has successfully produced its first set of medical doctors, who he said have been inducted into the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria, MDCN, in August this year.
“We produced our first set of medical doctors. The first set of students for our Bachelor of Medicine; Bachelor of Surgery programme (MBBS) successfully completed their course of study in the session having sailed through all the required statutory and professional accreditation requirements. All of them, 90 in number, were inducted by the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria on 12th August, 2026, and shall be presented their degrees on Wednesday, 23rd September, 2026,” he added.

title: Eric Stinton: A Staple Of Hawaiʻi’s Literary World Is Back
content:
Eric Stinton: A Staple Of Hawaiʻi's Literary World Is Back
The state’s longest-running reading series has returned. It is inspiring people to read, network and write.
By Eric Stinton
September 22, 2026 · 5 min read
About the Author
Eric Stinton is a writer and teacher from Kailua. You can follow his work through his newsletter at ericstinton.substack.com.
The state’s longest-running reading series has returned. It is inspiring people to read, network and write.
If you ask Sujatha Raman and Kristiana Kahakauwila how they became co-organizers of MIA Honolulu, the longest-running reading series in Hawaiʻi, they will tell slightly different versions of the same story. In both tellings, it started at the Association of Writers and Writing Programs conference in 2025.
“In my version,” said Kahakauwila, a celebrated author who directs the creative writing program at the University of Hawaiʻi Mānoa, “Sujatha had been talking about wanting to start a reading series.”
“There’s some truth that I wanted to organize it,” said Raman, a writer and non-profit consultant. In her version, she had been wanting to focus more on writing; attending the conference in the first place was a part of her mission to take her own work more seriously. Organizing a reading series, in her telling, “adds labor without adding pages.”
But while at the AWP conference, she attended a panel on – you guessed it – starting a reading series. Raman, who grew up in Singapore and lived in Brooklyn for 20 years before moving to Hawaiʻi in 2016, had already been organizing a weekly writing group at Hub Coworking Hawaiʻi.
“Anybody who wanted to write and just needed an hour of quiet space would come,” said Raman. “We’d write together and then hang out for an hour. It was really generative. So I said maybe we should provide this sort of space for readers.”
The idea stuck with her, so she reached out to several writers, including Kahakauwila. The connection felt like a sign. “I had already been thinking of restarting MIA,” said Kahakauwila.
MIA – which stands for Mixing Innovative Arts – started in 2009, the brainchild of Jaimie Nagle, then a PhD student at UH Mānoa who was looking for a place for artists to share work and hang out off campus. “I read in it during its second year, so I’d been there pretty early, and I loved the vibe, that it felt casual and community-based,” said Kahakauwila.
MIA continued under different organizers until 2020, when the pandemic sent it into a dormancy that, after five years of silence, started to seem permanent. (Yours truly was one of the readers at its final 2020 event; the extent to which I am to blame for its hiatus is unclear.)
In October 2025, Kahakauwila and Raman co-organized the first MIA event since February 2020. MIA was officially, ahem, back in action.
Before that, the literary community had deeply felt its absence. They had lost a space for writers and readers to gather just as Hawaiʻi’s literary renaissance was beginning to blossom.
Hawaiʻi Writers On The Rise
Hawaiʻi has always punched above its literary weight class, with writers such as Kiana Davenport, Lois-Ann Yamanaka, Susanna Moore, Chris McKinney and Kaui Hart Hemmings publishing to significant critical and commercial success in the 90s and 2000s.
But in the last six years, Hawaiʻi writers have been publishing acclaimed, award-winning books nearly every year. Just last week, two Hawaiʻi writers – Keala Kendall and Tae Keller – were longlisted for the National Book Award for Young People’s Literature.
“There’s an incredibly vibrant literary scene, and there has been since the 1820s,” said Kahakauwila, whose 2013 story collection “This Is Paradise” is a monument of contemporary Hawaiʻi literature. “The problem wasn’t finding enough people. It’s a really exciting time. 2026 has been a year of great books from Hawaiʻi.”
So far in this year alone, Shay Kauwe’s “The Killing Spell” and Alicia Upano’s “Everything To The Sea” have been published by Big Five publishers; both Kauwe and Upano read at MIA earlier this year.

And more great books being written means more book-launch events, filled with celebratory energy that has inspired the newly-resuscitated MIA.
“There’s a jubilance at these events, a joy, because you’ve worked so hard on this book and here you are finally presenting it to the world,” said Raman. “But maybe you’re working on your first draft, maybe you’re in between books and you want to try out something different, or maybe you’ve been writing and writing but have only published a couple of short stories. I just felt the need to meet more people who are reading and writing.”
‘People Just Can’t Stop Talking!’
MIA holds readings every second Thursday of the month at OurSpace Hawaii, with different themes for each gathering. “Literary happenings should be like costume parties,” Kahakauwila said. “It’s a way to bring in writers from different communities.”
The March event, “Build Me A Bangka,” featured Filipino writers; the event from earlier this month was “Noir Night.” And when the opportunity arrives, themes are often seasonal, like February’s “Love & Other Disasters” for Valentine’s Day, and next month’s “What Whispers Back: Spinning Hawaiʻi’s Spooky Tales” for Halloween.
Writing, or art of any kind, is often a solitary, lonely pursuit, but having a space to share and enjoy that art with others – off-screen and in-person – taps into a deep, human need that our increasingly digitized world overlooks: the need for connection and community.
After the readings, people hang out, talk story, eat pupus, go out for drinks together. “Your world feels fuller,” said Kahakauwila.
“I’ve been surprised at how vibrant the social hour is after the readings,” said Raman. “It’s magnetic. People just can’t stop talking! They express all sorts of things, hidden desires to write. It’s lovely.”

title: Court grants default bail to six Ukrainians arrested for suspected links with Myanmar armed groups
content:
Court grants default bail to six Ukrainians arrested for suspected links with Myanmar armed groups
Although they had been arrested under UAPA, the NIA chargesheet accused them only of immigration offences.
A Delhi court on Wednesday granted default bail to six Ukrainians who were arrested by the National Investigation Agency in March for allegedly having links to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar that are hostile to India, PTI reported.
Default bail is granted when an investigating agency fails to complete its probe and file a chargesheet within the statutory period while an accused is in custody.
On Friday, the court granted default bail to Matthew Aaron Van Dyke, a United States citizen who is also accused in the case.
The seven foreigners were allegedly involved in supplying weapons and military equipment to ethnic armed groups operating in Myanmar, as well as providing them with training.
On September 8, the NIA filed a chargesheet against them for illegally entering, staying and moving in India under the 2025 Immigration and Foreigners Act.
Although they had been arrested under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, the agency had only accused them of immigration violations in the chargesheet.
Special NIA Judge Prashant Sharma on Wednesday discharged the six Ukrainians under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, noting that the Foreigners Regional Registration Office had compounded the offences against them by imposing a fine of Rs 5.5 lakh on each, reported PTI.
Compounding of offences is a legal settlement mechanism where an accused person pays a specific sum of money to the authorities to avoid criminal prosecution.
The six persons were granted bail against a cash bond of Rs 1 lakh each.
Van Dyke had been arrested on March 13 at Kolkata airport. On the same day, Ukrainian citizens Petro Hurba, Taras Slyviak and Ivan Sukmanovskyi were arrested at Lucknow airport, while Marian Stefankiv, Maksim Honcharuk and Viktor Kaminskyi were held at Delhi airport.
Investigators had alleged that they had entered India on valid visas, but later travelled to Mizoram without the mandatory restricted area permit. They were also accused of entering Myanmar and meeting ethnic groups hostile to India.
Officials alleged that the individuals received drone deliveries from Europe while in Mizoram.
